subject: Computing

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 12, the very last unit of Year 3 Computing at Ehel Academy. Be a Problem Solver. In this unit they pull their skills together around one big idea: every algorithm and every program has an input and an output. An input is the data we give to an algorithm — what we put in, or what starts it off. An output is the result — what comes out after the steps have run. This unit names that idea and uses it to plan and build small programs. You already know inputs and outputs from everyday life, even without the words: press a button on the remote (input) and the channel changes (output); put fruit in a blender (input) and out comes a smoothie (output).
learningPath: Preview the goals, key words and the tools you will use
Read the concept explainers and study the code examples
Follow the methods and worked examples
Build the activities, debug your work and play the games
Apply, explain and finish the Unit Project and Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Computing 0672 — Stage 3 Teacher & Parent Guide, Activity Sheet and Mini-Project. Teacher-directed prose was rewritten into learner-facing explainers so the unit teaches with no adult present.

outcomes: Identify the input(s) and the output of an algorithm, in everyday activities and in written steps.
Understand that an input is the data we give to an algorithm, and an output is the result of processing it.
Create a simple algorithm that turns an input into an output, such as a number machine.
Break a big job into small steps in the right order (decomposition).
In Scratch, use an event block (green flag, sprite clicked, key pressed) as the input that starts a program.
In Scratch, build a program that resets a sprite to its starting costume and position.
Plan, test and fix a program — find a bug, correct it, and run it again.

concepts.title: Inputs and outputs are everywhere
concepts.explanation: Every algorithm has an input and an output. The input is the data we give it — what we put in, or the thing that starts it. The output is the result we get out. Inputs and outputs are all around us, every single day. Watch. I press this button — that is the input, the thing I put in.
concepts.example: The television changes channel — that is the output, the result. Input goes in, output comes out.
concepts.checkYourself: A common slip is to name the machine (the blender) as the input — gently steer you to the thing we put in (the fruit) and the result that comes out (the smoothie). Can you point to the input (what goes in / what starts it) and the output (the result)?

concepts.title: Break a big job into small steps
concepts.explanation:
A good problem solver takes a big job and breaks it into small steps in the right order. Those steps are an algorithm. An algorithm can have one or more inputs and it gives an output. Naming the inputs and the output helps us check the algorithm does its job.

When a job feels big, we do not panic. We break it into small steps, one at a time. That is what a problem solver does.
concepts.example: Find one real example of break a big job into small steps around you, or on a device you use. Say out loud what it is and why it fits.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you point to which steps are the inputs and which is the output? Can you list the steps in a sensible order? Do not worry about perfect wording — the thinking is what matters.

concepts.title: Plan a reset (before we code)
concepts.explanation:
Before we build a program, a problem solver plans it on paper first. Today we plan a special kind of algorithm: a reset. A reset sends a character back to exactly where it started, so we can play again. In Scratch the input for a reset is clicking the green flag, and the output is the character jumping to its starting spot.

Think of a board game. After each go, we put the counter back on Start.
concepts.example: Our Scratch character needs the same thing, or the next go begins in the wrong place. Clicking the green flag is the input; going back to the start is the output.
concepts.checkYourself: When you fill in the Frog plan, do the coordinates match the numbers given? Watch the minus signs.

concepts.title: Code the reset in Scratch
concepts.explanation: Now we turn our plan into a real program. In Scratch we join coloured blocks. The block at the very top that starts everything is called an event block (it is shaped like a hat). The event block is our input. The blocks under it are the outputs — the actions that happen. Delete the cat sprite, add the Horse sprite (the Add Sprite button, bottom right), and choose the Farm backdrop. Open Scratch at scratch.mit.edu and click Create on the projector. By now you know the Scratch screen well.
concepts.example: Do it yourself: code the reset in Scratch. Work through it slowly, then check what you did against the explanation above.
concepts.checkYourself: Can you pick the right event block for each input? Can you click the green flag to test the reset? Can you find a block by its colour group and join it to the stack?

concepts.title: Test it and fix the bugs
concepts.explanation: A real problem solver does not stop when the program is built. You test it — run it and watch carefully — and if it does not do what the plan said, they hunt for the bug and fix it. Finding and fixing a bug is called debugging, and it is the most important problem-solving skill of all. Even the best coders get bugs. A bug is not a failure — it is a clue.
concepts.example: We run it, watch what really happens, compare it to our plan, and find the one block that is wrong. It should send the Horse to the bottom-left, but the Horse goes to the wrong place
concepts.checkYourself: When something is wrong, Can you look back at your plan and check block by block, instead of starting over? Do you test by running the program, rather than assuming it works? Praise calm, careful debugging.

selfAssessment: I can identify the input(s) and the output of an algorithm, in everyday activities and in written steps.
I can understand that an input is the data we give to an algorithm, and an output is the result of processing it.
I can create a simple algorithm that turns an input into an output, such as a number machine.
I can break a big job into small steps in the right order (decomposition).
I can in Scratch, use an event block (green flag, sprite clicked, key pressed) as the input that starts a program.
I can in Scratch, build a program that resets a sprite to its starting costume and position.
I can plan, test and fix a program — find a bug, correct it, and run it again.
